raw_response:
## Recommended direction

For this rebuild, I would start with **Laravel**, retain the existing business rules behind a small application-service layer, and use **Blade/Breeze plus Livewire** for account screens and ordinary interactions. This recommendation is an inference from your existing PHP experience and the need to finish quickly. It does not assume that ten-year-old PHP or Perl code can be dropped into a modern framework unchanged.

Keep the drag-and-drop behavior in the browser and persist completed moves to the server. If the component editor needs substantial local state, previews, undo, or many interactions before saving, **Vue through Inertia** is the alternative I would investigate before committing to Livewire throughout.

The following candidates are ranked by practical usefulness to the described site. Some are the application framework and others cover a specific feature; they are not eight competing complete solutions.

1. **Laravel 9, with Breeze as a starting point** — [framework release notes](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/releases) and [starter kits](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/starter-kits). Laravel provides a PHP application structure for the database-backed account and component/group workflows, while Breeze scaffolds account authentication. That keeps the main implementation language familiar and gives you a concrete starting point. The official release table dates Laravel 9 to February 8, 2022 and states that it requires PHP 8.0 or later. Adapt and test the old business logic behind the new controllers; this is not an automatic migration of old PHP, Perl, database schemas, or user passwords. The present starter-kit documentation is not independently dated to the question's cutoff.

2. **Livewire 2** — [official quickstart](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/quickstart/). Livewire components combine PHP classes and Blade views and update a page after actions without a full reload, making it a useful option for selection controls, forms, account settings, and group-management screens. This can limit the amount of unfamiliar frontend architecture you must learn. I would still let a browser-side drag library handle the motion itself, and send completed edits to the server; a highly stateful editor needs a prototype before assuming Livewire is the best fit. The opened versioned documentation is undated, so its cutoff status remains unknown.

3. **SortableJS** — [public source and README](https://github.com/SortableJS/Sortable/blob/master/README.md). Its cross-list dragging, grouping options, drag events, and item-ID serialization are directly relevant to moving selected components between saved groups. You would map a completed drop to an authenticated server operation containing the component ID, group ID, and order. SortableJS supplies the browser interaction; it does not supply user accounts, database persistence, or business-rule validation. Thousands of saved items also do not imply that every item should be rendered simultaneously: search, paging, or a limited working set is an application design decision. The opened source is the current master branch, so I have not backdated its exact capabilities.

4. **Laravel Excel 3.1** — [export quickstart](https://docs.laravel-excel.com/3.1/exports/). Its documented export object and controller download flow can produce the user's Excel file from application data, avoiding a custom spreadsheet writer. Define explicit export columns and scope the query to the requesting user's permitted records and groups. The simple example loads a collection; large exports need separate memory and execution-time assessment. This is an export package rather than the application framework, and the opened 3.1 documentation has no verified publication date.

5. **Inertia.js with Vue and Laravel** — [Laravel's documented Inertia integration](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/starter-kits) and [Inertia routing reference](https://v1.inertiajs.com/routing). Laravel documents React/Vue pages connected through Inertia while retaining server-side routing and controllers. This is a plausible alternative when the drag-and-drop editor deserves richer browser-side state but you still want to keep PHP on the server. It introduces a modern JavaScript component model and build workflow, which adds learning work. I would select this approach or the simpler Blade/Livewire direction according to a prototype of the hardest editor interaction. The Inertia page opened without readable body text, so the functional claim is verified through Laravel's primary documentation; exact historical availability of the inspected integration documentation is unverified.

6. **Chart.js** — [official documentation](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/). Its browser chart rendering can display aggregated component-use counts returned by the backend, which covers the statistical graphs in the requirements. Compute the business meaning of usage and the aggregate counts on the server; the chart library does not provide those rules. Its canvas rendering also means chart styling and accessibility require deliberate implementation. The usable documentation page is marked last updated August 7, 2023, after the January 10, 2023 cutoff; I retain it as later evidence, not as proof of the exact feature set available at the question date. Two attempts to inspect a 3.9.1 source failed.

7. **Laravel Cashier for Stripe** — [Laravel 9 billing documentation](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/billing). Cashier provides documented subscription and payment workflows that could cover the prepaid service if Stripe fits the existing payment arrangement. The document also lists single-charge and checkout paths, so the payment model should be chosen explicitly rather than assuming that “prepaid” means a recurring subscription. A stored-credit balance or a custom entitlement ledger remains your application logic, and changing payment providers may outweigh the package's benefits. The live versioned documentation was opened, but its publication date was not established.

8. **Django 4.1** — [framework overview](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/intro/overview/) and [dated release announcement](https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2022/aug/03/django-41-released/). Django's model, database, routing, and administrative-interface facilities make it a credible alternative for a database-oriented application. The official release announcement establishes availability on August 3, 2022. For your specific deadline, I rank it below retaining PHP because Python would require translating or separately exposing existing PHP/Perl business logic and learning a different stack. Its administration interface also does not replace your custom customer-facing drag-and-drop editor.

## What I would build first

Prototype one complete workflow: sign in, search the component catalogue, select a component, drag it into a group, reload and verify persistence, then export that user's data. Use that prototype to choose between Livewire and Inertia before rebuilding every screen. Preserve the existing business decisions in explicit functions or services, with representative old inputs and outputs available to check the migration.

A component, a user's saved selection, a group, and a membership/order record are distinct concepts; modeling them separately is my suggested starting design, not a claim about your existing schema. Keep the catalogue searchable and save changes by stable IDs. Add graphs and billing after that core workflow works.

This research identifies useful building blocks, not a tested implementation or a delivery-time guarantee. I found no evidence establishing that any candidate has already been deployed successfully for this particular site.
